title: KoreLumina — Master OS - KoreLumina Reconstruction Plan

messages.content:
Yes—and I actually think this is the ideal time.
I wouldn't train a model yet, but I would start building what I'll call the KoreLumina Learning System. By the time KoreLumina reaches production, it will already have months of engineering knowledge instead of starting from zero.
During implementation
Every engineering task becomes training data.
For example, today's work:
RT-002

Goal:
Create Runtime Project Registry

Files Changed:
runtimeRegistry.ts
registry.ts
projects.ts

Reason:
Consolidate Runtime source of truth.

Outcome:
Success

Tests:
Passed

Architecture:
RUNTIME_PLATFORM_SPECIFICATION_V1
That is an excellent training example.

Record everything
As you implement KoreLumina, capture:
Architecture


Specifications


ADRs


Design decisions


Domain model


Contracts


Engineering


Git commits


Pull requests


Reviews


Refactors


Bugs


Fixes


Runtime


Runtime logs


Crash reports


Recovery actions


Metrics


AI


User request


Plan


Generated draft


Final accepted implementation


Human edits


This is far richer than just storing prompts.

Build an Engineering Memory
Instead of:
LLM
Build:
LLM

+

Engineering Memory

+

Repository Intelligence

+

Runtime Knowledge

+

Architecture Knowledge

+

Decision History
Eventually, the LLM becomes just one component.

Give the agent access to the entire repository
As KoreLumina grows, the agent should understand:
Architecture

↓

Specifications

↓

Repository Graph

↓

Type Graph

↓

Dependency Graph

↓

Runtime State

↓

Project State

↓

Git History

↓

Issue History

↓

Engineering Decisions

↓

Current Task
Then it isn't "reading files"; it understands the system.

Let it observe you
This is something most companies don't have.
Every day it can observe:
Problem

↓

Investigation

↓

Root Cause

↓

Architecture Decision

↓

Implementation

↓

Validation

↓

Commit
Over hundreds of tickets, it starts recognizing your engineering style and standards.

Build it as another KoreLumina platform
I'd add a new platform to the architecture:
Knowledge Platform
Responsibilities:


Repository Knowledge Graph


Engineering Memory


Architecture Memory


Runtime Memory


ADR Memory


Semantic Search


Code Embeddings


Decision Graph


Learning Pipeline


This platform serves both the AI Platform and the Engineering Platform.

Long-term vision
Eventually the flow becomes:
Repository Imported

↓

Repository Intelligence

↓

Knowledge Graph Updated

↓

Architecture Graph Updated

↓

Runtime Graph Updated

↓

Engineering Memory Updated

↓

Agent Learns

↓

Future Suggestions Improve
No retraining required for many improvements—just a richer knowledge base.

When to fine-tune
Only after you have:


Thousands of repositories


Tens of thousands of accepted code changes


Large numbers of validated fixes


ADR history


Runtime diagnostics


Deployment history


At that point, you can fine-tune a model on data that is unique to KoreLumina.

One enhancement I'd make to your roadmap
I would move this work earlier than I originally suggested.
Instead of waiting for production, add a parallel workstream during implementation:
Knowledge Platform (Parallel Track)


Sprint 1: Engineering Memory


Sprint 2: Repository Knowledge Graph


Sprint 3: Architecture Memory


Sprint 4: Runtime Memory


Sprint 5: Semantic Search & Embeddings


Sprint 6: Agent Context Builder


This work doesn't interfere with building the Runtime or AI Platform. It quietly accumulates high-quality engineering knowledge from day one. By the time KoreLumina reaches production, your future engineering agent will already understand the platform's architecture, history, conventions, and implementation decisions, giving it a substantial head start over an agent that begins learning only after launch.
How do we set that up now

I would start today, but do not start with model training.
Start by building the infrastructure that will eventually train and power the agent. Think of it as building the agent's brain before teaching it.
This becomes Phase 0, running in parallel with Phase 1 (Universal Runtime).

New Platform
I would add one implementation project:
Knowledge Platform (KP)
Its job is not AI.
Its job is to remember everything.

Step 1 — Create the Knowledge Store
Under the runtime workspace, create a new area:
runtime/
    knowledge/
        architecture/
        adr/
        runtime/
        repository/
        engineering/
        commits/
        tasks/
        embeddings/
        conversations/
        telemetry/
This becomes KoreLumina's memory.

Step 2 — Record Every Ticket
Every ticket creates a structured record.
Example:
JSON{
  "ticket": "RT-002",
  "platform": "Runtime",
  "goal": "Create Runtime Project Registry",
  "files": [
    "runtimeRegistry.ts",
    "registry.ts"
  ],
  "decision": "Registry becomes Runtime source of truth.",
  "validation": "Passed",
  "commit": "88cb79e"
}
That alone is valuable training data.

Step 3 — Repository Knowledge
When a repository is imported, automatically generate:
Repository

↓

Framework

↓

Languages

↓

Dependencies

↓

Architecture Graph

↓

Route Graph

↓

Component Graph

↓

API Graph

↓

Database Graph

↓

Manifest
Store it permanently.
Never analyze the same repository from scratch again.

Step 4 — Runtime Knowledge
Every runtime event becomes memory.
Example:
Runtime Started

↓

Project Loaded

↓

Port Allocated

↓

Vite Started

↓

Crash

↓

Recovery

↓

Restart

↓

Success
Eventually the agent recognizes recurring patterns.

Step 5 — Architecture Knowledge
You've already written this.
Instead of treating it as documentation, ingest it into the Knowledge Store.
Example:
Runtime Platform Specification

↓

Sections

↓

Responsibilities

↓

Contracts

↓

Events

↓

Entities

↓

Relationships
Now the agent can query:

"Who owns Preview?"

without scanning Markdown.

Step 6 — Engineering Memory
This is the biggest asset.
For every implementation:
Problem

↓

Investigation

↓

Root Cause

↓

Specification

↓

Implementation

↓

Validation

↓

Commit

↓

Result
Over time, this becomes an engineering playbook.

Step 7 — Build a Knowledge Graph
Instead of documents, think in terms of relationships.
Project

↓

Repository

↓

Component

↓

Route

↓

API

↓

Runtime

↓

Draft

↓

Commit

↓

Issue

↓

ADR
Every node connects.
This becomes far more powerful than plain vector search.

Step 8 — Add Embeddings
Later, index everything.
Examples:


Architecture


ADRs


Runtime logs


Commits


Specifications


Source code


Tickets


Repository manifests


Now the system can answer semantic questions like:

"Show me every runtime restart bug."

or

"Where else have we solved this?"


Step 9 — Build the Context Builder
This is the component that feeds AI.
Instead of sending the whole repository:
User Request

↓

Context Builder

↓

Knowledge Graph

↓

Repository Graph

↓

Architecture

↓

Relevant Files

↓

Runtime State

↓

History

↓

LLM
This dramatically improves relevance.

Step 10 — Only Then Train
Months later you'll have:


thousands of tickets


runtime telemetry


architecture


engineering decisions


accepted code


rejected code


refactors


fixes


That becomes your training dataset.

Where this fits in KoreLumina
I would actually update the platform architecture slightly:
Customer Experience

↓

AI Platform

↓

Knowledge Platform

↓

Repository Intelligence

↓

Universal Runtime
The AI Platform becomes a consumer of knowledge rather than its owner.

What I would implement first
After RT-002, I would start a parallel epic:
KP-001
Knowledge Store

KP-002
Architecture Ingestion

KP-003
Repository Knowledge

KP-004
Runtime Knowledge

KP-005
Engineering Memory

KP-006
Context Builder

KP-007
Semantic Search

KP-008
Knowledge Graph
None of these require training a model, but each one increases the intelligence of every future AI interaction.
One recommendation
I would make the Knowledge Platform a first-class platform in KoreLumina, alongside the Runtime and AI Platform, rather than treating it as an internal utility. Long term, it becomes the institutional memory of the entire system. Every repository, runtime event, architectural decision, engineering task, deployment, and AI interaction contributes to it. When you eventually build your own engineering agent, it won't just have a language model—it will have years of accumulated engineering knowledge specific to KoreLumina. That is a much stronger competitive advantage than simply training a custom model.
Draft a handoff to the new conversation to implement this before continuing implementation works

This is the direction I would take. The key difference is that we are not pausing KoreLumina implementation. We are implementing a foundational platform that every subsequent phase will use.
